faq.q: How do I find a unique name for my Indian Leopard?
faq.a: Unique names often come from less obvious sources: scientific names (e.g., Panthera), foreign languages, obscure mythology, musical terms, or personal memories. Observe your Indian Leopard's quirks — a distinctive behavior or marking can inspire a one-of-a-kind name nobody else will have.

faq.q: Should my Indian Leopard's name reflect their species?
faq.a: It can, but it doesn't have to. Some owners love species-referential names (''Stripes'' for a zebra, ''Fin'' for a fish), while others prefer names that contrast playfully (''Tiny'' for a large animal). Let your Indian Leopard's individual personality guide you more than their species label.

habitat: Indian leopards inhabit virtually every habitat type across the Indian subcontinent — from the tropical rainforests of the Western Ghats and Himalayas to dry deciduous forests, scrublands, grasslands, and even the semi-deserts of Rajasthan. They are remarkably adaptable, often living in close proximity to human settlements — leopards have been documented in the outskirts of Mumbai, Delhi, and Bengaluru. Their habitat overlaps extensively with tigers, but leopards tend to avoid direct competition by hunting smaller prey and utilizing different areas and times.
diet: Indian leopards are opportunistic carnivores with one of the most diverse diets of any big cat. They prey on spotted deer, sambar, barking deer, wild boar, langur monkeys, hares, peafowl, and smaller mammals. In human-dominated landscapes, they prey heavily on domestic dogs, goats, and livestock. They are adaptable ambush predators, stalking within 5-10 meters before a final explosive charge. They frequently cache kills in trees to protect them from tigers, hyenas, and wild dogs — a behavior requiring immense strength.
behavior: Indian leopards are solitary and territorial, active primarily at night in human-dominated areas and at dawn and dusk in protected forests. They are among the most successful large predators at coexisting with humans, often going completely unnoticed in agricultural and suburban landscapes. Males maintain territories that overlap those of multiple females. Females give birth to 2-3 cubs in secluded dens — caves, thickets, or even abandoned buildings. Cubs learn to hunt through observation and practice, staying with their mother for 12-18 months. Despite their fearsome reputation, they are secretive and avoid humans when possible.
facts: Indian leopards exhibit the greatest variation in coat color of any leopard population — from pale yellow in arid regions to deep gold in forests, and including black (melanistic) variants commonly called 'black panthers.' They are the most common large predator in India, with an estimated 12,000-14,000 individuals. The melanistic variant is particularly common in the dense, humid forests of the Western Ghats and Northeast India. Leopards have been living alongside humans in India for millennia, appearing in ancient art, folklore, and religious iconography.
naming: Indian leopard names might reflect their Indian heritage or distinctive spots. Consider names like Chitra (spotted in Sanskrit), Bagh (tiger in Hindi — used for leopards too), Shimla, Ghat (after Western Ghats), Tendua (leopard in Hindi), Raja (king), Kali, or Kabini (after the famous leopard territory).
